title: 2026 Isthmus General Election voter guide - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: Una versión en español de esta guía está aquí . The top race in Wisconsin may be the battle for governor, but there are other high-stakes contests too. The outcome of Wisconsin’s congressional races in play could help determine which party controls Congress in 2027. Control of the state Legislature could also be up in the air, with some of the first opportunities to test the competitiveness of newly drawn maps. There’s plenty to sort through on the ballot, and plenty to help you develop a plan to vote. This guide breaks down what voters need to know, whether they plan to vote early or on Nov. 3. We have included links to both our election coverage and to other trusted sources of information. This fall’s partisan election may bring some upsets. But with this resource, there should be no surprises when you’re at the ballot box. Representative in Congress District 2 First elected in 2012, Democratic U.S. Congressman Mark Pocan is running unopposed for what will be his eighth term representing south-central and south-west Wisconsin. Of the eight U.S. House races in Wisconsin, this is the only district where there’s just one candidate on the ballot. Governor/Lieutenant Governor It’s an open race for Wisconsin’s next governor. U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany is the Republican nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley is the Democratic nominee. Isthmus profiled this race in our October cover story . The two candidates will meet for just one debate, at 7 p.m. on Oct. 21, which will air live on WISN and stream on wisn.com (those in Madison can watch on WKOW). Topics will include the cost of living, taxes, immigration enforcement, data centers and election security. In Wisconsin, governors don’t get to pick their lieutenant governors. David Varnam , a former mayor of Lancaster in southwest Wisconsin, is running on the Republican ticket. Sarah Godlewski , Wisconsin secretary of state and former state treasurer, is running on the Democratic ticket. Attorney General It’s déjà vu in the race for attorney general. Republican Eric Toney , the Fond du Lac County district attorney, is again challenging Democrat Josh Kaul for the position. Kaul was first elected attorney general in 2018, and was re-elected in 2022 after facing a challenge from Toney, who has been elected four times as DA. Secretary of State There are not two but three candidates on the ballot this election. Republican and MAGA activist Jay Schroeder is running to make the secretary of state the chief election official of Wisconsin; contrary to most other states, the office does not oversee elections in Wisconsin. Democrat JoCasta Zamarripa is a Milwaukee Common Council member and former state legislator. Pete Karas , a former Racine Common Council member, is running as a Wisconsin Green candidate to end “the undemocratic two-party stranglehold on our elections.” State Treasurer Republican incumbent John S. Leiber is running for another four-year term as state treasurer. He faces Democrat Yee Leng Xiong , a nonprofit executive and former Marathon County board supervisor. This will be the second election under Wisconsin’s freshly redrawn legislative maps. Though Republicans have led both chambers of the legislature for 16 years, Democrats could be poised to take control of the state Senate or, less likely, the state Assembly. In total, 14 legislative Republicans are not running for re-election. State Representative State representatives serve two-year terms, and all 99 seats in the Wisconsin Assembly are on the ballot. The following races fall within the Dane County area: Assembly District 42 : In this district in northern Dane County and southern Columbia County, incumbent Democratic Rep. Maureen McCarville will face Republican Keith F. Miller , a farmer, Army veteran, and Columbia County supervisor. Assembly District 46 : In this district covering eastern Dane County and western Jefferson County, incumbent Democratic Rep. Joan Fitzgerald will face Republican John Donohue . Assembly District 47 : This district south of Madison includes the cities of Fitchburg and Stoughton. Incumbent Democratic Rep. Randy Udell will face a challenge from Republican Sandy Bakk . Assembly District 48 : This district northeast of Madison includes the city of Sun Prairie. Incumbent Democratic Rep. Andrew Hysell will face a challenge from Republican Mark Kjorlie . Assembly District 51 : This district represents western Dane County, all of Iowa and Lafayette counties, and parts of Grant County. As he seeks his seventh term in office, incumbent Republican Rep. Todd Novak faces a dual challenge from Democratic conservation warden Ben Gruber and the American Solidarity Party’s Nathan Tataje . Assembly District 76 : Comedian, food service worker, and Madison Ald. Dina Nina Martinez Rutherford emerged from a crowded primary to be the Democratic nominee in this deeply blue district representing Madison’s isthmus and east side. She is strongly favored to win. If she does, she’ll become the first transgender member of the state Legislature and will replace outgoing Rep. Francesca Hong. Republican Nina Chat, a Madison resident and parent who does not have a campaign website, tells Isthmus she is running a word-of-mouth campaign focused on education reform, lower property taxes, and enhanced charter school options. Assembly District 77 : Incumbent Democratic Rep. Renuka Mayadev will face a challenge from Republican Jane McCormick . Assembly District 78 : Incumbent Democratic Rep. Shelia Stubbs will face a challenge from Republican Henry Johnson, a student at UW-Madison. Assembly District 79 : Incumbent Democratic Rep. Lisa Subeck will face a challenge from Republican John Fons . Assembly District 80 : Incumbent Democratic Rep. Mike Bare will face a challenge from Republican Simran Arora . Assembly District 81 : Incumbent Democratic Rep. Alex Joers will face a challenge from Republican Mark S. Maier . Wisconsin state senators serve four-year terms. Odd-numbered seats are on November’s ballot. Senate District 17 : This district includes southwest Dane County, as well as Green, Lafayette, Iowa, Grant and Crawford counties. Howard Marklein , a co-chair of the Joint Finance Committee, is one of the few Republican incumbents running for re-election. Democrat Jenna Jacobson , a current state representative, is challenging Marklein as he seeks his fourth term in office. Senate District 27 : In this district that represents northwest Dane County, Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein , a Democrat, is running unopposed for re-election. Dane County Sheriff Democrat Kalvin Barrett is running unopposed for re-election as Dane County sheriff. He was first appointed to the office in 2021 and elected to a full term in 2022. Dane County Clerk of Circuit Court Clerks of court administer circuit courts, including maintaining a court’s records and finances. Jeff Okazaki , appointed in 2024, is running unopposed for his first full term. Voters across Wisconsin will see three constitutional referendums on the ballot. Each measure was approved by the state Legislature in successive sessions. Unlike other legislation, constitutional amendments cannot be vetoed by the governor if they are approved by voters. Question 1 concerns the governor’s partial veto power. It asks: “Shall section 10 (1) (c) of article V of the constitution be amended to prohibit the governor, in exercising his or her partial veto authority, from creating or increasing or authorizing the creation or increase of any tax or fee?” Question 2 concerns the emergency powers of public health officials in places of worship. It asks: “Shall section 18 of article I of the constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency?" Question 3 concerns the prohibition of discrimination and preferential treatment. It asks: “Shall section 27 of article I of the constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration?" The State Democracy Research Initiative has published detailed explainers on each of these proposed constitutional amendments. Wisconsin Watch has also published an explainer with political context. I’m already registered Vote by mail: If you are registered to vote, you can request an absentee ballot and return the completed ballot by mail, at an absentee ballot drop box, or in-person to the City Clerk’s Office at 210 Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd. Your request for an absentee ballot must be received by the City Clerk’s Office by 5 p.m. on Oct. 29 — though if you request it that late, it may not come in time for Election Day — and your completed ballot must be received by the City Clerk’s Office by 8 p.m. on Election Day for it to count. The earlier you send it off, the better. The City Clerk’s Office recommends allowing at least one week for your ballot to travel through the mail. City of Madison voters may also bring completed ballots to drop-off sites throughout the city through Nov. 2 at 5 p.m. You may also bring your absentee ballot to your polling place on Election Day. Vote early in-person: Early in-person voting, also called in-person absentee voting, begins Oct. 20 and ends Oct. 31. To vote early in person, you will need to bring a photo ID. For Madison voters, the City Clerk’s Office maintains a list of in-person absentee voting locations and the hours they are open. Voters outside Madison can consult check MyVote for more information. I need to register You must be registered in order to cast a ballot. You also must be registered at your current address unless you have lived there for fewer than 28 days. You can register to vote at the polls on Election Day, but registering early can save time and avoid confusion. No matter what options you choose to register, you will need to provide proof of residence. The Madison City Clerk’s Office maintains a list of what counts as valid proof of residence , such as a pay stub or a bank statement, which can be shown in either paper or electronic form. Madison voters can register in-person in the City Clerk’s Office, or at the front desk at a Madison public library or other city agency, until Oct. 20. From Oct. 20 to Oct. 30, Madison residents can register at an absentee early voting site . Registration at early voting sites ends before early voting does because voter registration is not allowed on the Saturday, Sunday or Monday before Election Day. Register online or by mail: Online and mail registration closes on Oct. 14, per a state law that only allows in-person registration for 20 days before an election. I just moved. Where do I vote? Wisconsin state statute requires you to be a resident for 28 days prior to voting in a district. In most cases, if you moved after October 6, 2026, then you’ll want to vote from your immediate previous address. If you moved on or before October 6, you’ll need to register to vote at your new address. I am involved in the carceral system. Can I vote? It depends. If you have been convicted of a felony, you can vote once you are “off paper,” meaning you have completed probation, parole, or extended supervision. If you have been charged but not yet convicted, you can vote. You still must register to vote. If you have been convicted of a misdemeanor you can still vote in most instances, even if you are incarcerated. The Wisconsin ACLU addresses more situations for justice-involved people. I need help getting to the polls. If you’re in Madison, Union Cab provides free rides to the polls on Election Day only. Rides are only available from home to polling place to home. These cannot be scheduled in advance. Call 608-242-2000 on Election Day for a ride. The city of Fitchburg Senior Center can provide free rides to the polls for Fitchburg residents age 60 or older, on Election Day. You need to schedule your ride before Election Day. Call 608-270-4290. I need other help with voting. The League of Women Voters provides resources ( en español ) on voter eligibility and registration. They provide help in Spanish or English on general voting questions through their helpline: 608-285-2141. Wisconsin has some of the most decentralized elections of any state in the country. There are more than 1,800 local election clerks. One of them is your local municipal clerk, who is typically happy to answer your specific voting question. Look up your local clerk. The Wisconsin Elections Commission launched the Election Information Hub earlier this year. It provides a detailed calendar of dates and deadlines, election resources , statistics and data , a FAQ , and more explainers. The Commission’s Voter Information Center is also helpful. MyVote Wisconsin , a service of the Wisconsin Elections Commission, allows you to preview what’s on your ballot based on your address. You can also find your polling place and track your ballot . The League of Women Voters maintains Vote411.org , which allows you to see races and candidates on your ballot. The group’s “ Candidate Answers ,” which surveys candidates on the ballot, is also available. Ballotpedia offers a ballot lookup tool in English and Spanish. Enter your address to find who’s on your ballot. Wisconsin Watch has compiled a voting guide for federal and state candidates. Enter your address to find information about the candidates. Wisconsin Public Radio surveyed listeners for questions, then posed those questions to the candidates for governor, attorney general, secretary of state, treasurer, U.S. House of Representatives and the state legislature. You can read their answers in its voting guide . The Recombobulation Area, a Milwaukee-based independent outlet, has provided a rundown of every race in both the state Assembly and the state Senate . WUWM has produced a cheat sheet on how this midterm election is politically consequential up and down the ballot. Who is funding the candidates? County candidates’ campaign finance reports are here . Campaign finance reports for state candidates are available using Sunshine , the state’s new campaign finance system. You do not need to login or register to use the tool. Federal campaign finance reports are searchable at the Federal Elections Commission. The nonpartisan group OpenSecrets also maintains an easy-to-use database to track campaign contributions for federal and state candidates. How do election results get reported? All vote tallies on Election Night are unofficial, and there is no official website where results are reported. Instead, county clerks and central count locations post unofficial results online. You can view those results here ; results in Dane County will be posted here . In the weeks following the election, local clerks, county boards of canvassers, and then the state Elections Commission will certify the results.

title: 10 bites from Madison budget briefings - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: How much does it cost to keep a city running? About $477.5 million next year, according to Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway’s executive operating budget proposal . City leaders will be putting the finishing touches on next year’s operating and capital budgets for the next month. As one step in that process, city department heads make their case for agency funding to members of the finance committee, who then make their budget recommendations to the full council, which is set to vote on a final budget the second week of November. Isthmus tuned in to two evenings of briefings earlier this week. The mayor’s operating budget proposal is largely a “cost to continue” budget, which means keeping funding fairly static, and there are few new big-ticket items. In introducing her budget proposal earlier this month, the mayor highlighted an expedited body-worn camera program for Madison police, partially funded by a $350,000 grant from the Madison Community Foundation; a city-wide compensation study; and annualized investments in recently launched initiatives like a tenth city ambulance and the recently opened Imagination Center library . At the finance committee, departmental leaders shared statistics from Results Madison , a city initiative that is new to this year’s budget process and aims to give the public more data for city outcomes. They also shared budget bites. Here are 10 of those. 1. The city clerk’s office is storing election equipment just off the Beltline. A reorganization following significant staffing changes has “helped tremendously,” says Deputy Clerk Gretchen Coleman. But there was some confusion when Ald. Mike Verveer pressed for more details on the clerk’s temporary storage plan for election equipment. Could that equipment be permanently housed at the county’s new elections center , being built at the former Ale Asylum brewery on Pankratz Street? “We don’t have a signed agreement,” interjected Mayor Rhodes-Conway, but the city is “in conversation” with the county clerk’s office, so stay tuned on this one. Total proposed operating budget for the clerk’s office: $3.63 million. ( Jump to city clerk briefing .) 2. The city assessor says she’s saving you $500. 960 property owners objected to their property assessments in 2025, and went on to have them reviewed by the board of assessors. From there, just 91 went on to a second round at the board of review. 20 went on to sue in circuit court, and every one of those 20 was a commercial property. “The untold story in these numbers is the prevention of value shifting out of the commercial class,” city assessor Michelle Drea said. In a review of appeals from 2020 to 2025, she estimates $1.5 billion would have “shifted out” of the commercial class if her office hadn’t defended its assessments. That equates to $30 million in taxes residential owners would have had to pay — or about $500 per residential parcel. Total proposed operating budget for the city assessor: $4.13 million. ( Jump to city assessor briefing .) 3. The parks division is nixing the postcard. The parks division will stop mailing postcards for public meetings, and nix its postage budget for them, said Superintendent Eric Knepp.“If you were to do the math on total [public meeting] attendees and assumed that everyone came because of a postcard — which is not true — it’s about $43 per person,” Knepp added, promising to enhance other ways of delivering that information. Total proposed operating budget for the parks division: $23 million. ( Jump to parks division briefing .) 4. 911 calls for medical help are outpacing population growth. Since 2021, there’s been a 31% increase in 911 calls for EMS, fire, or special rescue — nearly double the rate of population growth in that time, said Madison Fire Department Chief Chris Carbon. And last year, there were 1,047 instances when the fire department had either one or zero ambulances available to respond to a 911 call. He expects that number to decrease now that the fire department has added a tenth ambulance . Total proposed operating budget for the fire department: $83.4 million. ( Jump to fire department briefing .) 5. Developing area plans takes one quarter of total staff planners’ time. In 2022, the city’s planning division embarked on a project to carve the city into 12 slices, and develop area plans for each slice. So far, planning staff have completed four area plans, but it takes a significant amount of dedicated staff time, said planning division director Meagan Tuttle. The office is also working on how it will comply with a new “truth in planning” law approved by the state Legislature in April. Total proposed operating budget for the planning division: $4.32 million. ( Jump to planning division briefing .) 6. Software costs rose by almost $1 million. In a nearly 10% increase over last year, rising vendor prices are sending software costs soaring as data moves from city servers to subscription-based cloud services. “By moving to the cloud, we’re just supporting technology in a different way,” says IT director Sarah Edgerton, “but it’s not getting rid of all of our infrastructure.” Just this summer, city IT staff completed four migrations, including for its asset management and timekeeping systems. Total proposed operating budget for IT: $12.8 million. ( Jump to information technology briefing .) 7. Regional bus service at the redeveloped State Street ramp is delayed. The project at 415 N. Lake St. is finished, and the garage officially opened in late August. The regional transportation terminal will also feature bus service from four companies, but opening that service is dragging past a mid-October expected launch. Parking division director Stefanie Cox says at least one company will begin operating in November. Total parking utility budget: $20.4 million. ( Jump to parking division briefing .) 8. It’s a “mixed bag of challenges” for the bus system. Madison Metro Transit General Manager Jamie Acton was pressed over instances of cancelled bus routes. Electric buses have had more battery issues than anticipated, and diesel buses are needing more repairs as they reach the end of their life, she said, adding “mechanically, we’re having a hard time keeping up.” On a rosier note, plans are in place to buy a few new hybrid buses in 2027. Total Madison Metro Transit budget: $92.5 million. ( Jump to Metro Transit briefing .) 9. It’s a state limit on budget growth, not revenue limits, that’s squeezing this year’s budget. The amount the city can raise each year is capped by state levy limits, which restrict how much the city can raise property taxes in order to raise revenue. In recent years, city leaders have blamed levy limits for squeezing the city budget, but this year’s challenge is different. Instead, it’s related to state limits on expenditures under a program called ERIP . Roughly speaking, the city would be penalized by more than $9 million if the budget grows beyond the rate of inflation. That’s a problem, since city expenses have grown faster than inflation. Before 2026, the expenditure limit was much higher than the levy limit. But in the 2026 budget and again in the 2027 budget, expenditure restraints are a much greater constraint. ( Jump to budget overview .) 10. The tax rate is going down, but your property bill will still go up. The city has a historically low tax rate this year, said city finance director Dave Schmiedicke, but explaining how your bill will still go up takes some math-splaining. That difference accounts for a slight 1.2% reduction in the mill rate, which is the number an individual’s property tax value is multiplied by in order to arrive at your share of property taxes. title: Madison police monitor voted out in marathon council meeting - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis — The Madison Common Council voted Wednesday morning to remove the city's interim independent police monitor following a lengthy meeting. In a tense Common Council meeting that began Tuesday evening and saw public comment last over seven hours, Glass was voted out in a 14-6 vote. The vote was nearly postponed to Thursday because the council had to clear the chamber by 7 a.m. A motion to move the vote failed at 6:30 a.m. Aye No Following the vote, newly-elected Police Civilian Oversight Board chair Devon Snyder said he was "deeply disappointed" by the decision to fire Glass and called for continued conversations about what police oversight in Madison will look like moving forward. "What does this decision mean for those community members? What does it mean for the independence of this office? What assurances does our community have that independent oversight will remain independent when it becomes uncomfortable or politically difficult," he asked in a statement. "These are not questions we can afford to ignore." About 140 people registered to speak during public comment. For hours, speakers urged alders to keep Glass in her position. The emotion in the room was evident as some speakers cried or angrily criticized the mayor and city attorney while defending Glass and the city’s police oversight system. Others spoke in favor of terminating Glass, but at times struggled to be heard over the crowd. When David Blaska spoke in support of the resolution, audience members booed and shouted. The disruption prompted the mayor to warn that she would adjourn the meeting if the room did not settle down. Alder Ochowicz introduced the resolution to terminate the appointment of Glass on Oct. 6. Common Council President Sabrina Madison, District 3 Alder Derek Field, District 5 Alder Regina Vidaver, District 9 Alder Joann Pritchett, District 10 Alder Yannette Figueora Cole, and District 13 Alder Tag Evers signed onto the resolution as cosponsors shortly after it was introduced. A few days later, Alder Noah Lieberman and joined the resolution and Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford appeared to show support for it as well. Snyder spoke out during Tuesday's meeting in opposition of firing Glass. "I believe terminating Meeka would be a mistake." Snyder said. "What concerns me tonight is the precedent," if a leader charged with independent oversight can be removed whenever controversy arises then what message are we sending to the next independent monitor." Former board chair Maia Pearson said neither Ochowicz nor any cosponsors of the resolution reached out to the PCOB prior to it being introduced. The resolution cited "concerns with the actions of the Interim Independent Monitor in completing her responsibilities, including but not limited to serving as hiring manager for the permanent Independent Monitor" as reason for removing Glass. Only two alders, District 18 Alder Carmella Glenn and District 12 Alder Julia Matthews, objected to the introduction of the resolution. Speaking to the Council, Glass defended her work as monitor thus far and detailed her fracturing relationship with Madison Police Chief John Patterson, who she accused of being misleading. Glass also accused the mayor and city attorney of lying about her and maintained her position that she hasn't broken any city rules, contradicting a review published by the city attorney's office. She accused the city's HR director of sharing medical information about her staff with members of the council and said that was one of several aspects that led to a breakdown between her and the director. Glass also had a somewhat heated exchange with Alder Pritchett, at one point refusing to answer questions about her stance on co-morbidities citing statements Pritchett made that Glass said tied her to Madison's police union. Wednesday's vote follows a tense string of exchanges between Glass and city officials. In the summer, footage posted to Facebook showed Glass saying she "will burn this city down" following a physical altercation with Madison police. The Green Bay Police Department investigated the altercation and referred charges against Glass to the Dane County District Attorney. In September, a Dane County judge granted a Madison police officer's temporary restraining order against Glass stemming from the altercation. Glass also sued the Madison Police Department for records tied to the death of Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by an officer. That litigation is ongoing. The Police Civilian Oversight Board said in an evaluation published this week that Glass "performed at a high level." The board looked at Glass' performance in areas like statutory compliance, leadership and communication. The board's evaluation went against a review of Glass published earlier this month by City Attorney Michael Haas' office, which documented a communication breakdown between the monitor and Haas as well as multiple instances where Glass' office potentially violated city rules. The review accused Glass of failing to follow budget instructions, hiring outside counsel and investigators without city-approved contracts and not adhering to Wisconsin's Open Meetings Law. Haas told the council during Tuesday's meeting that his office looked into Glass' conduct and work after receiving questions from alders and the public. He did not say what specific alders contacted him. While answering questions from alders, Haas was repeatedly shouted at by members of the public. He and Alder Glenn sparred over which city rules Glass might have broken, with the two going back-and-forth about the handling of contracts with outside counsel and investigators. Hours before the meeting began, Haas accused Glass of leaking confidential information in the death of Richard Johnson that was later posted on Alder Glenn's Facebook page. Around the same time, Glass' office announced it had hired outside counsel to represent the grandmother of Tony Robinson, who was shot and killed by Madison Police Officer Matt Kenny in 2015. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. title: Editorial | Elect Jenna Jacobson and a progressive Legislature - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom. Sign up for the Opinion Roundup newsletter for weekly Madison and Wisconsin viewpoints. Southwestern Wisconsin needs dynamic representation in the state Senate, and Jenna Jacobson has the experience and the enthusiasm to provide it. A Democratic member of the state Assembly, Jacobson’s been a leader in the fight to defend rural schools and Universities of Wisconsin campuses. She’s committed to preserving and funding the threatened hospitals and clinics vital to the health and safety of the towns, villages and small cities of Iowa, Lafayette, Grant, Green and Crawford counties, along with the portion of western Dane County that make up the 17th District. And as a veteran member of the Oregon Village Board, Jacobson understands the importance of getting sufficient shared revenues to Wisconsin communities as part of the broader fight to reduce the burden of property taxes. Jacobson’s bipartisan record, and her excitement about representing the causes and concerns of southwest Wisconsin in the Senate, stand in stark contrast with conservative Republican incumbent Howard Marklein. Marklein has served in the Legislature for the better part of two decades, since the days when he used his positions in the Assembly and Senate to advance former Republican Gov. Scott Walker’s assaults on workers and their unions, fair elections and the environment. Walker is long gone, having been ejected from office in 2018 by voters who recognized the damage he was doing to Wisconsin’s most vulnerable communities. But Marklein remains as a steady defender of Walker’s legacy. Instead of working in a meaningful way with Democratic Gov. Tony Evers to benefit southwest Wisconsin, Marklein has used his powerful position as co-chair of the legislative Joint Finance Committee — according to a recent report by Wisconsin’s UpNorthNews — to undercut “more than 1,600 of Evers’ proposals, including funding for childcare, school meals, clean water, and paid family leave.” His woeful environmental record, as tallied by the nonpartisan Wisconsin Conservation Voters, shows he's voted for conservation proposals just 15% of the time, earning him a “Conservation Dishonor Roll” placement. Jacobson, in contrast, has voted with environmental causes 100% of the time, earning her the distinction of “Conservation Champion.” Marklein failed to act on adequately funding the Division of Vocational Rehabilitation, which helps people with disabilities find employment and attain academic success. That failure led to a catastrophic waitlist of more than 7,600 that won’t clear until next June. He didn’t respond to multiple requests for an explanation when the Cap Times editorial board reached out. Marklein also faced criticism this year for failing to adequately defend against the closure of Wisconsin’s rural schools and UW system campuses. But his failures are really part of a broader disengagement from the values and concerns of the voters he is supposed to represent; indeed, this fall, he didn’t even bother to fill out the nonpartisan League of Women Voters of Dane County questionnaire for legislative candidates. Jacobson offers an energetic alternative to the incumbent. She’s campaigning everywhere from Mount Horeb to Monroe, Dodgeville to Platteville. She’s visited every corner of the district and offered detailed plans to fight in the Legislature for public education, the environment, family farms, healthcare, childcare, affordable housing and women’s rights. And, if Democrats retain the governorship and — thanks to fair maps — win control of the Senate and Assembly, she’ll be in a good position to implement an agenda that truly serves southwest Wisconsin. We’re highlighting the race in the 17th because it could well be the contest that flips control of the Senate to the Democrats, a change that is critical to achieving effective progressive governance over the next four years. But every Senate contest matters, and we are proud to endorse a pair of Democratic incumbents who represent the region: District 15’s Mark Spreitzer , who has been a leader in the fight to expand access to healthcare; and District 27’s Dianne Hesselbein , the Democratic leader in the chamber and a strong advocate for regulating data centers, holding down utility costs and codifying a woman’s right to choose. Hesselbein says that with fair maps and a strong slate of candidates, “Wisconsin Democrats are on the precipice of winning a trifecta — meaning we’ll have real power to deliver for working families across Wisconsin.” She’s right. But that trifecta requires voters in Dane and surrounding south-central Wisconsin counties to choose Democrats to flip control of the Assembly away from the Republicans who, for 15 years, have relied on Walker-era gerrymandering and special interest money to maintain their destructive control of the chamber. With that in mind, we’re endorsing the reelection bids of able and experienced Democratic incumbents Maureen McCarville (District 42), Brienne Brown (43), Joan Fitzgerald (46), Randy Udell (47), Andrew Hysell (48), Renuka Mayadev (77), Shelia Stubbs (78), Lisa Subeck (79), Mike Bare (80) and Alex Joers (81). In the 51st District, which stretches from western Dane County across much of southwestern Wisconsin, we reiterate our strong endorsement last week of Ben Gruber , who will be a legislative leader and absolute champion for rural schools and hospitals. In the race to fill the open District 50 seat, we encourage voters to choose Bill Oemichen , the president of the New Glarus School Board, who faces Republican Jon Aleckson. We’re impressed with elements of Aleckson’s “Restore Wisconsin Plan” that propose innovative strategies for developing affordable housing. But Oemichen’s more comprehensive approach, and his experience on the school board and as a professor who teaches about law and local government, means that he will hit the ground running as a representative for Green County and southwestern Dane County. In Madison’s 76th District, Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford will be a great successor to state Rep. Francesca Hong. She’s on the progressive side of issues ranging from data centers to housing and LGBTQ+ rights. She’ll represent her district well and keep Democrats focused on economic, social and racial justice.

The Madison Common Council fired Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass early Wednesday morning, voting 14-6 to end her appointment effective immediately after a meeting that ran more than 12 hours. Glass was hired in December 2025 mainly to run the search for a permanent monitor. Ten months later, a city review found no approved job description, no job posting and no candidates. The final vote came with no debate. The meeting had stretched to nearly 7 a.m., and the Municipal Court needed the room, Madison365 reported . Alders had sat through nearly seven hours of public testimony and four hours of questions to city staff. Two motions to recess until Thursday failed before Council Vice President Carmella Glenn moved to call the question. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said 140 people registered to speak. All but three spoke against firing Glass, Madison365 reported. Voting to fire Glass were Council President Sabrina Madison and Alders Will Ochowicz, Joann Pritchett, Bill Tishler, Michael Verveer, Regina Vidaver, Tag Evers, Derek Field, Yannette Figueroa Cole, John Guequierre, Badri Lankella, Noah Lieberman, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford and Sean O’Brien. Glenn and Alders Ellen Zhang, Barbara Harrington-McKinney, Julia Matthews, Davy Mayer and Devine Nzegwu voted no, WMTV reported . Hours before the meeting, Madison posted a blunt message on her council blog for people who called the effort racist. “You know and I know that race is being weaponized when accusations of racism are used to shut down discussions about terminating IIPM Glass,” Madison wrote . Gelembiuk is a longtime activist on police violence issues in Madison. More than 200 people have circulated and signed a petition urging council members to reject the proposal to fire Glass, with some calling it a “transparent attempt to punish someone who has tried to hold the police accountable.” Mark Treinen contributed to this report.

title: City council fires Madison’s independent police monitor, draws shouts of ‘shame’ - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: Chali Pittman Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass answers questions during an all-night city council meeting Oct. 20. Elsa Ruiz delivered a personal appeal to city council members Tuesday night as they considered a controversial vote to terminate an extended contract with interim independent police monitor Aeiramique Glass. “First and foremost, I would like you to vote for Miss Glass,” said Ruiz, the mother of Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by a Madison police officer nearly three months ago. “She has been doing a superb job in her position,” added Ruiz, calling Glass “someone I need desperately in my corner.” But, as dawn broke, the council voted 14-6 to terminate Glass’ extended contract as interim independent monitor. Voting no were Alds. Ellen Zhang, Carmella Glenn, Barbara Harrington-McKinney, Julia Matthews, Davy Mayer and Devine Nzegwu. After the vote, the dozens who remained in the council chambers shouted “shame” at the alders who had voted to end the contract. As the council wrapped up, alders and city staff hustled to clear the room to allow for setup for municipal court. Uniformed police officers intervened as some protestors confronted city alders. The resolution to remove Glass, who became the city’s interim police monitor in December 2025, was introduced from the floor Oct. 6 by Ald. Will Ochowicz. The resolution reverses the extension of Glass’ appointment that the council approved June 9 . Under that extension, Glass would have worked through March 2027, or departed earlier if the position were filled. It also places the office of the independent monitor under the supervision of Karen Kapusta-Pofahl, chief of staff for the Common Council, and engages experts from the National Association for Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement for their help in finding a permanent monitor. Those opposed to the resolution argued that it violates the 2020 ordinance that created the independent monitor position. The ordinance states that the monitor reports directly to the Police Civilian Oversight Board, and that “the monitor shall act as directed by the board.” It also states, “No city employee or official shall attempt to use their political or administrative position to unduly influence or undermine the independence of the monitor.” Going into the meeting, there were eight co-sponsors of Ochowicz’s resolution : Council President Sabrina Madison, Alds. Yannette Figueroa Cole, Tag Evers, Regina Vidaver, Derek Field, Joann Pritchett, Badri Lankella and Sean O’Brien. Some explained their reasoning ahead of time. “Trust is low between the Common Council, the PCOB, and the public,” Ochowicz wrote in an Oct. 15 blog post. “I hope that people understand that what I am doing is what I think is best for the city. What is going on right now is clearly not working, and we need to do better.” Vidaver wrote that Glass failed to follow work rules — including neglecting to submit paperwork for contractors or adhering to telework and family leave policies — and exhibited a “lack of discernment and objectivity.” “This has been by far the most challenging decision I have had to make as alder,” wrote Ald. Noah Lieberman in a blog post . Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, in explaining how she had changed her mind “no less than 50 times,” wrote that Glass “exhibited behavior that gives me pause and causes me to question her judgment as a leader who is employed by the city.” Public comment dominated eight of the meeting’s 12 hours, as those crammed into council chambers frequently interrupted, heckled and insulted the city staff, alders, and those who spoke in favor of firing Glass. In total, the resolution drew 177 people registered in support, 318 against, and three registered neither for nor against, according to city staff. It also drew 109 pages of written comment ahead of the meeting. A protest led by the UW-Madison chapter of Students for a Democratic Society converged on the City-County Building at the start of the meeting, as a police drone monitored overhead. So many people showed up that the staff opened an overflow room one floor above. On the ground floor, half a dozen uniformed officers tuned in to the proceedings from a reception desk, ready to be called into council chambers if need be. The firing of the independent monitor, the overwhelming number of speakers said, symbolized many things. It was “evil,” “procedural corruption,” “retribution and retaliation,” “frankly ridiculous,” an attempt to “sweep police murder under the carpet,” support of “a racist system,” a “slap in the face,” and “an urgent rush to push a Black woman out of her job.” Crowds drowned out the few speakers who defended the firing of the monitor, including conservative blogger David Blaska and police advocate Bonnie Roe. A few speakers backed the termination on process grounds. “No matter how pure her intentions,” said Edward Montasaros, one of Glass’s core responsibilities was to recruit a permanent hire, and he pointed to the little that had been done. Greg Gelumbiak, the office’s data analyst, spoke at the speed of an auctioneer during public comment, declaring he was in his eighth day of a satyagraha, a hunger strike in an “appeal to moral principles.” “If this resolution is passed, I will continue my fast,” Gelumbiak said, arguing that the allegations against the police monitor were distorted and lacked context. “Monitor Glass is being subject to a political lyching.” Former alders who helped establish the groundwork for the police civilian oversight committee, and the role of the monitor, urged their successors to support the independence of the monitor position. “I’m just so furious with this council,” said Brenda Konkel, who served as alder from 2001-2009. “If you can’t respect community voices, can you at least read my email, and think about legislative intent?” Konkel called on alders to remember that the civilian oversight board and independent monitor were designed to be independent of the city council and the mayor. “Honor that intent,” she added. Former longtime Ald. Marsha Rummel, calling herself the “ghost of Common Councils past,” described “the hundreds of hours” previous alders had invested in creating the monitor and oversight board. “We gave you a gift,” she said, conceding that there are still “some things to figure out.” She cautioned: “I don’t think you have the authority to terminate the appointment.” Rummel represented the Williamson Street area when Tony Robinson was killed in 2015 by police officer Matt Kenny. Kenny was not charged with any crime, and remains employed by the Madison Police Department. In 2017, the city of Madison settled a $3.35 million civil rights lawsuit with Robinson’s family. Chali Pittman Elsa Ruiz, mother of Corey Ruiz, said Glass is 'someone I need desperately in my corner.' Robinson’s grandmother, Sharon Irwin, has continued to seek justice. In 2023, assisted by a team of attorneys, Irwin sought to use a little-known state law to compel a judge to issue a criminal complaint if a district attorney refuses to prosecute. The effort failed. Hours before Tuesday’s meeting, Glass announced she had hired attorney Damon Etawlyah to represent Irwin before the Police and Fire Commission in her grandson’s case. It’s the first time the monitor’s office has appointed an attorney to represent a complainant. Speaking in front of the council, Irwin paced back and forth, admonishing alders for ignoring her pleas for action and calling them “colonizers.” “And you guys call yourselves moral? You’re not even close to moral,” she said. “For 11 years, you ignored me.” On Monday, the civilian oversight committee announced it had conducted a performance review of Glass and found she had “performed at a high level across every category.” “Board members identified significant strengths in her leadership, communication, commitment to independent oversight, community engagement, and dedication to advancing the mission of civilian police oversight,” the board said in a news release. The review was not statutorily required for an interim monitor. “The evaluation also identified opportunities for continued growth, including rebuilding relationships with key stakeholders, expanding data-driven oversight efforts, strengthening public communication strategies, and continuing efforts to secure the resources necessary for the office to fully conduct its mission. Board members emphasized that many of these challenges arise within a complex environment involving multiple governmental agencies and institutional barriers.” The review follows an Oct. 2 “ employment review ” prepared by City Attorney Michael Haas. The document states it aims to “respond to inquiries from the public and alders” by outlining the interim monitor’s duties and responsibilities set forth in the job announcement and appointment letter, employment law, and more. After public testimony, and over the course of some three hours, alders posed questions to city staff, including Haas, police Chief John Patterson, and Glass. The discussion reflected the lack of clarity over how the monitor’s office differs from a traditional city agency and what that means in terms of requirements to follow city human resource rules and contracting procedures, among other things. Glass outlined her difficulties: “It’s not about not wanting policy to adhere to and how we function. It’s about who it flows through,” she said. “There is currently no pathway that does not lead back to the mayor or to the Common Council.” [Editor's note: A previous version of this story incorrectly said the council would take up the rest of its agenda Oct. 22. That motion failed; alders instead voted to adopt the remainder of the agenda.]

title: After All-Night Meeting, Madison Council Fires Police Monitor Who Said City Rules Didn't Apply - Wisconsin Right Now
text: Buy Me a Coffee Glass also told alders she would not apply in a competitive process but was open to being appointed to the permanent job directly. The Madison Common Council fired Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass early Wednesday morning, voting 14-6 to end her appointment effective immediately after a meeting that ran more than 12 hours. Glass was hired in December 2025 mainly to run the search for a permanent monitor. Ten months later, a city review found no approved job description, no job posting and no candidates. The final vote came with no debate. The meeting had stretched to nearly 7 a.m., and the Municipal Court needed the room, Madison365 reported . Alders had sat through nearly seven hours of public testimony and four hours of questions to city staff. Two motions to recess until Thursday failed before Council Vice President Carmella Glenn moved to call the question. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said 140 people registered to speak. All but three spoke against firing Glass, Madison365 reported. Voting to fire Glass were Council President Sabrina Madison and Alders Will Ochowicz, Joann Pritchett, Bill Tishler, Michael Verveer, Regina Vidaver, Tag Evers, Derek Field, Yannette Figueroa Cole, John Guequierre, Badri Lankella, Noah Lieberman, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford and Sean O’Brien. Glenn and Alders Ellen Zhang, Barbara Harrington-McKinney, Julia Matthews, Davy Mayer and Devine Nzegwu voted no, WMTV reported . Hours before the meeting, Madison posted a blunt message on her council blog for people who called the effort racist. “You know and I know that race is being weaponized when accusations of racism are used to shut down discussions about terminating IIPM Glass,” Madison wrote . The interim job was built around one main task. Glass was to serve as hiring manager for the next permanent monitor, and the job description said the person in the interim role could not apply for the permanent one, WMTV reported in September. The council unanimously extended her appointment in June, through March 31, 2027, to give the search more time. It didn’t move. An Oct. 2 employment review from the Common Council office counted the gaps, Evers wrote on his council blog : no approved position description, no job posting, no community outreach, no hiring committee and no candidates sent to the Police Civilian Oversight Board or the council. At the meeting, Glass put the blame on the board she reports to, saying it never wrote a permanent job description. “I can not post a job description that does not exist,” she said, Madison365 reported . Glass also told alders she would not apply in a competitive process but was open to being appointed to the permanent job directly. City Attorney Michael Haas said no ordinance or hiring document allows a direct appointment without a posting and a competitive search. “I don’t know where that idea came from,” Haas said. Lieberman, who wrote that his vote would disappoint many of his allies in the push for police reform, called the stalled search the chief reason he voted yes. He said Glass never publicly ruled out seeking the job and did nothing to correct supporters who pushed for her to get it. “I do not have faith that IM Glass would effectively pursue the recruitment and appointment of someone else to the role of permanent IM if she were to continue to serve in the interim role,” Lieberman wrote before the vote. Alders also said Glass refused to follow the city’s administrative procedure rules, known as APMs, which cover contracting, purchasing, leave and workplace conduct for every city employee. In an email to Haas, Glass wrote, “We do not have to comply with [Administrative Procedure Memoranda] other than what we do in good faith when I feel comfortable doing so,” Wisconsin Right Now reported . The ordinance that created her office says otherwise on contracts. When the monitor hires outside help, such as an investigator, the monitor “shall follow all City of Madison contracting requirements,” the ordinance states, as Lieberman quoted it . Haas gave alders two examples at the meeting. Glass retained an attorney to subpoena records from the Madison Police Department, and Haas said every attorney working for the city needs a written contract vetted by several departments. She also hired forensic pathologist Dr. Victor Weedn to review the autopsy of Richard Lee Johnson, who died in police custody in 2024. Haas said Weedn told him he had a written contract and that it was never properly approved. An Aug. 31 memo from Haas and the city’s finance, human resources and IT directors listed more problems, Madison365 reported . It said Glass hired contractors outside city purchasing rules, turned in her office’s budget request late, missed the mayor’s budget meeting and failed to properly notice board meetings. The office asked for about $781,158 for 2027. Rhodes-Conway said it was the only agency that did not submit a 2% reduction and did not meet budget deadlines, WMTV reported . Evers summed up the case against her in September, during a debate over a $28,500 funding request for her office that the council rejected. “IM Glass and her office have traded impartiality and objectivity for the passion of an activist. In so doing, she has torched OIM’s credibility,” Evers said, WMTV reported . Glass’s backers, including the oversight board that supervises her, argued the council had no power to fire her. City ordinance gives the Police Civilian Oversight Board the job of recruiting, hiring and supervising the monitor, with council confirmation. It does not mention firing. It also bars any city official from using their position to “unduly influence or undermine the independence of the Monitor,” Madison365 reported . “You are in direct violation of your own ordinance,” board Chair Maia Pearson said of the council. Pearson also said the Oct. 2 review was not a real performance evaluation. The board did its own review of Glass at her request and planned to file it with city human resources, she said. The board has said the City Attorney’s document is not the official evaluation, and Glass has disputed the review on a Facebook livestream, WMTV reported . Haas told Madison365 it was “not logical” to think the council could extend an interim appointment but not revoke it. In his opinion, he wrote, the resolution is legal and enforceable. Ochowicz’s resolution called Glass’s failure to complete essential duties a breach of contract. Glass told Madison365 she never signed an employment contract with the city. Glenn defended Glass during September’s funding debate. She described meeting someone “educated” who “knew her stuff, and question the system,” adding, “That’s what we’re supposed to be doing,” WMTV reported . The night brought one more twist. Glass had shared privileged emails between the City Attorney’s Office and the police department with Glenn, a revelation that came out the day before the vote. Glass said she felt she had to share some of them to fight the “lies” being told about her, Madison365 reported . Matthews, who also voted no, questioned how the review was built. She pointed out that it highlighted only one meeting with Police Chief John Patterson that Glass canceled because of illness. Patterson said he and Glass met monthly for most of her tenure and that some meetings were canceled for scheduling conflicts or illness, including one he canceled himself. The fight over Glass sharpened after a Madison police officer shot and killed Corey Ruiz in July. On Aug. 4, as the city cleared a protest encampment set up after the shooting, a police drone recorded Glass in a physical altercation with an officer. She was wearing a shirt with the city logo that identified her as the Independent Police Monitor. A separate video that circulated online appears to show Glass saying she would “burn the city down,” WKOW reported . “Any time a city employee is calling for violence, I think that’s really disturbing,” Rhodes-Conway said. In September, a Dane County judge granted a four-year harassment restraining order to a Madison police officer who said Glass swatted at and pushed the officer several times during the Aug. 4 confrontation. Glass asked to reschedule the hearing the morning it was held. The request was denied, and she did not appear, WMTV reported . Patterson referred the Aug. 4 incident to the Green Bay Police Department for an outside investigation. Lieberman wrote on Oct. 15 that Green Bay police have recommended charges against Glass to the Dane County district attorney. The district attorney’s charging decision was still pending when he wrote. Lieberman wrote that the vote had nothing to do with the Ruiz case or her office’s report on the death of Richard Lee Johnson. That report concluded Johnson died of restraint-related cardiac arrest caused by police action, not cocaine poisoning as the medical examiner had found. Lieberman wrote that he and every alder he has spoken with believe the Johnson investigation should be reopened. Firing Glass does not close the Office of the Independent Monitor. Under the resolution, Common Council Chief of Staff Karen Kapusta-Pofahl will supervise the office’s staff until a permanent monitor is hired. She will also work with the Finance Department on a plan to bring in the National Association of Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement, a national group known as NACOLE, to help with next steps, Madison wrote . Kapusta-Pofahl told the council she will not conduct investigations herself. If one is needed while the search continues, she will look to hire an investigator, Madison365 reported . Madison still has no permanent monitor, more than 10 months after Glass was hired to find one. Table of Contents

title: State restrictions leave Madison facing growing budget gap, mayor says - The Daily Cardinal
text: Madison’s proposed 2027 operating budget would increase by 5.5% from 2026, but Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway told The Daily Cardinal state-imposed restrictions on local revenue and expenditures will continue to limit the city’s ability to fund services and address long-term budget pressures. The proposed budget requests $477.5 million, up from $ 452.5 million in 2026. The operating budget covers day-to-day services, salaries and department operations. Over the past five years, Rhodes-Conway said she has built a healthy fund balance, an unassigned pool of money that is typically spent on property tax increases and unexpected expenses. The fund is grown through the city making more revenue than is spent in the fiscal year. The city aims to save between 15% to 20% of the general fund for this unassigned sector per year, according to its 2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. The proposed 2027 operating budget draws more than $6 million taken from the fund balance, in part to account for property tax increases. Madison property owners are expected to pay around $7 more each per month on their property taxes in 2027. “We are actually above our target amount for the fund balance,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Our fund balance is growing. Right now, I’m not concerned about this level of use, but I would be concerned about anything that was much higher than the [$6 million].” The Madison fund balance was more than $158.7 million, over the 15-30% fund balance goal as of Dec. 31 2025. Rhodes-Conway said it is “a healthy place to be.” The City of Madison website notes “strict restrictions on any new services or programs” in 2027 to instead focus on “high-priority needs of the community.” These needs include violence prevention in the wake of the police shooting of Corey Ruiz in July 2026. Rhodes-Conway said she is overseeing the implementation of body cameras in the Madison Police Department, which received $350,000 for body-worn cameras through a community grant. The Office of the Independent Monitor, previously led by Aeiramique Glass, who was fired on Oct. 21 for concerns over her job performance, requested $781,158 for 2027 and received $432,328, according to the budget proposal. The Mayor also highlighted the Municipal Services Payment program, which could provide the city $13 million in reimbursements if enacted by state legislators. “Given the multibillion-dollar surplus in the state's coffers, this is a straightforward and achievable step no matter the political landscape in 2027,” Rhodes-Conway wrote in the budget release. She told the Cardinal if the city were to receive more state aid, it would most likely go towards easing the burden on property taxpayers. “If we have more long-term stable funding from the state, that might allow us to consider investments in new services,” Rhodes-Conway said. “As long as the state limits both the levy and our expenditures through the Expenditure Restraint Incentive Program (ERIP), even with new state funds, we’d have to be very careful about our spending.” ERIP limits how much cities can increase their spending year to year, threatening the loss of $7 to $9 million in state aid if the limit is breached. The City’s Cost to Continue, how much funding is required to maintain current city services with no growth or new departments, is currently $7.2 million above the ERIP limit. The city identified over $1 million in efficiencies — resource allocation and cost-saving practices — resulting from agencies each cutting 2% out of their budgets as proposed by the city, according to the Mayor. Rhodes-Conway said this approach to saving is not sustainable, however. She noted city agencies have been cutting percentages of their budgets for 15 years, saying their budgets can only shrink so much given inflation. “We have 10% less staff per capita than we did 10 years ago, and we have found a lot of efficiencies, but there’s not going to be a lot more,” Rhodes-Conway said. “It's going to be a diminishing amount year over year, so we need the state to give us additional revenue options and lift restrictions on the budget.” She said regardless of the partisan makeup of the incoming legislators and governor, she is hopeful the new faces will “understand the challenges that are facing local governments in Wisconsin.” “Every year cities around Wisconsin are forced to fill a structural deficit gap that is created by the state legislature,” Rhodes-Conway said. “We are not able to access other revenue sources, and the state funding for cities has essentially stayed flat.” Jane Dardik is the City News Editor. She has covered a wide array of Madison stories, including city elections, budgets and community development.

title: Madison rezones 4,000 properties to help home projects, cut paperwork - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. City leaders have changed the zoning for thousands of Madison properties in an effort to simplify permitting and allow more types of housing to be built in certain neighborhoods. By unanimous vote at this week's meeting, the City Council rezoned around 4,000 single- and two-family properties in “ planned development ” districts across the city. The goal of the measure was twofold, city staff said. For one, it is meant to streamline city rules for residents and staff. Homeowners in planned development districts previously had to go through additional steps to receive approval for home projects like adding a new deck, pergola or egress window. Such measures are allowed “by right” in other residential zoning districts, creating less paperwork for homeowners and reducing staff workload. For another, recent city zoning changes designed to facilitate the construction of accessory dwelling units and duplexes in many Madison neighborhoods — part of Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway’s “ Housing Forward ” agenda — did not apply to planned development districts. Under the new zoning, such structures are now permitted, subject to homeowners association rules and other covenants. “What we've found over time with these (districts) is that their set-in-stone zoning text doesn't change when (the City) Council changes our zoning code,” said Katie Bannon, the city’s zoning administrator, at a June public meeting . “It creates barriers to adapting housing over time because it's really stuck in place, and it leads to a more confusing and protracted review and approval process for property owners within these areas when they want to make improvements to their homes.” As an example, Bannon pointed to a case last year when city staff worked with a homeowner for nine months as they sought to build a shed. The homeowner, she said, had to do some “unconventional sleuthing” to find contact information for specific people listed on planned development district documents who could approve the shed. “Ultimately, those people didn't want to take action, so we had to make a zoning code change to allow the city to move forward,” Bannon said. “If one of these private architectural review committees is not responsive — some of them definitely are responsive — but that is another step that's required of a property owner.” The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. The change, first discussed this spring, affects properties across 16 of the 20 City Council districts. Most of the properties are toward the far east and far west sides of the city, and most were rezoned into “low” or “low medium” designations meant to match current development patterns. “Unlike upzoning, which allows additional density and more uses, or downzoning, which allows less density and fewer uses, this could be called a ‘horizontal rezoning’ in that these rezonings are not intended to significantly change the uses or density allowed and already existing on these properties,” a recent planning staff memo says. In some cases, properties within areas where city plans call for higher density zoning like medium residential or mixed use were zoned for “less intense” housing levels. “Considering the low-intensity development patterns that exist in these areas, staff believes that maintaining less intensive zoning in these areas is consistent with this recommendation,” the staff memo says. This city map shows the planned development lots that have been rezoned across 16 of the 20 City Council districts. Prior to the City Council’s vote, resident Nicholas Davies said the choice for lower density in such areas represented a missed opportunity to allow for more housing. “The city talks a good game about missing middle housing forms like small-scale apartment buildings, but why do you think it's missing?” he asked. Planned development zoning was a common tool in previous decades in Madison and across the country. From the 1970s to the 2000s, it allowed developers more flexibility in construction and planning. Planners have turned to this type of zoning less and less, though. In 2013, the city conducted a major overhaul of its zoning code. Public feedback around the new changes centered largely around the role of homeowners associations. In response to questions at a June public meeting, Bannon said the city is not party to any private covenants, and the homeowners association fees and restrictions would remain in place. “Valid private covenants may continue to be enforced by the parties,” she said. A full list of rezoned properties, along with maps of neighborhoods sorted by City Council districts, may be found on the city’s “rezoning planned development zones” webpage .

title: Letter | Proposed car wash a bad fit for Stoughton Road
text: Dear Editor: Dane County received widespread opposition to a proposed private equity funded Mr. Splash car wash and vacuum lot at Buckeye and Stoughton roads. Despite health and safety concerns from 170-plus community members, the Dane County Zoning Committee approved a conditional use permit for the project on Oct. 13, without independent traffic study or fact-finding efforts. Opposition to this high-capacity car wash, which would be surrounded by homes on two sides, was voiced at a Sept. 22 public hearing and via a petition signed by residents and endorsed by Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford. title: Rhodes-Conway not seeking reelection - The Daily Cardinal
text: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she is not seeking reelection, pointing to a toxic political culture, personal attacks and threats, including harassment and sexism, in a press release Oct. 23 Rhodes-Conway, who has led the city for seven and a half years, highlighted her administration's accomplishments, including bus rapid transit, housing additions, creation of the Community Alternative Response Emergency Services (CARES) mental health program and investment in renewable energy.  “When I ran for mayor, I expected to make sacrifices — but I did not expect the level of threats to myself, Council members, my staff, and my family,” Rhodes-Conway said in the release. “I did not expect our civic discourse to deteriorate so severely. And I did not expect the levels of implicit and explicit sexism to which I have been subjected to from the very beginning of my first campaign.” Rhodes-Conway won the mayoral election in 2019 and was reelected in 2023. She announced in July that she planned to seek a third term. A week after the announcement, Madison police Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson shot and killed Corey Ruiz . Rhodes-Conway received backlash for removing an encampment in Ruiz’s honor on Willy Street where he was shot. Her announcement to not seek reelection also follows a 12-hour Common Council meeting earlier this week, where members voted to terminate the appointment of Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass. According to the Bridging Divides Institute, which Rhodes-Conway cited in her statement, 76% of local officials said they were less willing to engage in at least one of several key political or civic activities, such as working on controversial issues or running for higher office, due to concerns about harassment and threats of violence.  Rhodes-Conway said overall hostility toward public officials threatens local democracy by discouraging people from pursuing public service, adding that recent toxic political culture has led to personal attacks, threats and harassment.  “I have always welcomed honest disagreement and invited community input, but over the years the balance has shifted from productive discussion to increasingly vitriolic, personal attacks from people who seem not to care about actually understanding and debating an issue,” she said. For her remaining time in office, Rhodes-Conway said she hopes Madison residents will engage across political differences, build relationships beyond social media and encourage more people to pursue public service. “I believe Madison wants to be the kind of community where anyone can safely step into leadership, and I believe that we can choose to make that a reality,” she wrote. The Mayoral race in April 2027 is contentious, with eight declared candidates, including former Madison Common Council President Syed Abbas, former Alder Brian Benford, One City Schools founder and CEO Kaleem Caire, Natalia Hacerola, Jonny Hinds, Marcus Robert Johnson, April Kigeya and Larry “Ace” Williams. Candidates have all emphasized different approaches to addressing Madison’s affordability challenges, public safety concerns and governmental relationships. The field is still likely to change before the Jan. 5 nomination paper deadline.   Abbas issued a press release on the mayor’s decision, writing that he respected her commitment to the city and acknowledging the threats she received.  “I am deeply troubled by the threats and personal attacks she has described. No one serving our community should have to fear for their safety or the safety of their family,” Abbas wrote. Caire also issued a press release , emphasizing the importance of community. “I join all Madisonians today in saying 'thank you' to Mayor Rhodes-Conway for the many years she has shared her talents with this community,” Caire said. The City of Madison did not respond to The Daily Cardinal’s request for further comment.

title: Editorial | Rhodes-Conway's exit highlights toxic political climate - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom. Sign up for the Opinion Roundup newsletter for weekly Madison and Wisconsin viewpoints. There will be much to say in the weeks and months to come about Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway’s decision not to seek a third term after a tumultuous eight-year tenure as the city’s top official. The mayor, a detail-oriented policy wonk who has, for the most part, ably managed Madison through some of the most challenging times in the city’s history, plans to stand down at the end of her current term in April. Rhodes-Conway won her first two terms by wide margins. And she was widely seen as a frontrunner in next spring’s municipal election contest. But Rhodes-Conway had her share of detractors — especially in recent weeks, as the City Council made the controversial decision to fire interim police monitor Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass — and she had already attracted more than a half-dozen challengers at an early stage in next year’s election campaign. Rhodes-Conway’s decided to end a planned reelection bid after experiencing what she described as heightened threats and harassment not isolated to a single political party. "Madison has long been home to impassioned and spirited debate," she said in a public statement Friday. "But it is not hyperbole to say local democracy is at risk, not just from MAGA and right-wing extremists in the federal and state governments, but from a toxic political culture that is transcending partisanship and ideology. We appreciate the mayor’s frankness about her concerns regarding the future of the public discourse in Madison, especially her reflection that she has "always welcomed honest disagreement and invited community input." But there has been a shift in balance, she noted, "from productive discussion to increasingly vitriolic, personal attacks from people who seem not to care about actually understanding and debating an issue. “How can any leader govern responsibly when personal attacks and baseless conspiracies carry more weight than facts? How can any mayor be effective when a difference of opinion is cast as unforgivable betrayal that justifies threats of violence?” Madisonians should pause and reflect on the concerns the mayor has raised. They parallel complaints from many public servants about the coarsening of our politics at the national, state and local levels. And, as the race to replace Rhodes-Conway picks up steam, everyone should look for ways to dial down the vitriol without diminishing the serious focus on issues such as housing affordability, transportation and police reform. To her credit, Rhodes-Conway has given the candidates and the community space to get things right. She’s signaled that she won’t seek reelection more than a month before the Dec. 1 date when contenders for municipal posts can begin circulating petitions to get on the ballot for the February primary and the April general election. We hope that a wide field of contenders will decide to step up, and that this will be a spirited — yet also thoughtful and respectful — competition. There has never been any question about the mayor’s love for Madison and her desire for the city to progress. Her decision to stand down on a schedule that will allow potential successors to outline their visions for that progress is commendable — as is her desire to see her term through to its conclusion in mid-April. This is a reminder that, whether people agree or disagree with her, Satya Rhodes-Conway has taken seriously her duties not just as a mayor but as a public steward for a great American city.

text: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway will not seek re-election, she announced in a blog post Friday afternoon . “I am immensely proud of what I and my team have achieved over the past seven and a half years as we have worked to make Madison a better place and to prepare the path for future success,” she wrote. “My tenure has been marked by unprecedented challenges including COVID-19 and a state legislature intent on taking away our funding and powers. Rhodes-Conway joined the Madison Common Council as an alder in 2007, succeeding Brian Benford when he decided not to run for re-election. She served two terms, stepping away in 2013. She defeated incumbent Mayor Paul Soglin in 2019, and won re-election over former deputy mayor and school board president Gloria Reyes in 2023. text: MADISON, Wis. -- On Friday, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would end her bid for reelection over threats and harassment. "The price of being in public office has gotten too high," Mayor Rhodes-Conway said in a TV-exclusive interview with News 3 Now's political reporter and "For the Record" host Elly Laliberte. The news broke amid rising threats against mayors, common council members, and other local officials around the country. In a report from the Brennan Center for Justice published in 2024, more than 18% of local officeholders said they experienced threats or attacks in the 18 months prior to being surveyed. That rate was 52% when it came to less severe forms of abuse, like insults or harassment such as stalking. "Local leaders often have fewer protective services than state or national leaders," said Nathan Kalmoe, who leads the Center for Communication and Civic Renewal at UW-Madison. Kalmoe's work focuses on public opinion and political behavior, including political violence. In explaining her decision not to seek reelection, the mayor said she thinks about her physical safety on a daily basis. Threats and harassment against officials isn't new. The mayor's announcement came shortly after members of Wisconsin's congressional delegation received suspicious mail. The announcement also came on the heels of calls from the Wisconsin Supreme Court for $3 million to make courthouses safer after there were 129 reports of security threats to circuit court judges in 2025. Chief Justice Jill Karofsky has said that threats to the judicial system have increased. Data shows that larger shares of women and elected officials of color report experiencing abuse. "The reality is that threats against officials are more likely to target people who are already underrepresented in government," Kalmoe said. The Brennan Center for Justice report also showed more than two fifths of local officeholders said they're less willing to run for reelection or higher office because of abuse. For women, that rate was approximately 50%. Mayor Rhodes-Conway referenced the challenges posed specifically for local officials of color and women who hold office in her statement. "These negative impacts are especially pronounced for women officials, minority officials, and new officeholders," the mayor said. Kalmoe said an unsafe environment for elected officials worsens outcomes for their constituents. "If politics feels so toxic, especially if it feels unsafe, it's going to make people less likely to want to participate in it.
