title: Rhodes-Conway reverses course, won’t seek a third term - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: Tommy Washbush Rhodes Conway: 'I'm gonna try and find something that's at least as fun as being mayor.' Citing "credible threats" to her safety and increasingly personal attacks on her character, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway has changed her mind and will not run for a third term. In a statement emailed on Friday afternoon, Rhodes-Conway said the job had been a "tremendous honor," but that she "did not expect the level of threats to myself, council members, my staff, and my family," nor did she expect the "implicit and explicit sexism to which I have been subjected to from the very beginning of my first campaign." First elected mayor in 2019, Rhodes-Conway announced in July that she would run for a third term. Her decision to drop out makes it an open race for Madison’s next mayor, and many candidates have already declared . Rhodes-Conway hasn’t endorsed anyone yet, and says she wants to see how the field develops first. The mayor sat down with Isthmus on Thursday to explain her decision, what she plans to do with the six months left in her term, her thoughts on independent police oversight, and what lies ahead next spring. The two-term mayor calls it the “best job I’ve ever had,” but says she is ready for a different kind of work, where she can serve her community without being its public face. This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity. Isthmus: Why did you decide not to run for re-election? Mayor Rhodes Conway: There are a lot of reasons. Everyone who's in public service pays a price. For me, the price has gotten too high. Can you expand on that? Everybody who's an elected official — and even some folks that are not, but work for government — expect people to disagree with you. You expect things to be hard. But over the time that I have been in office, it has gotten increasingly personal. I would say mean, cruel, even. The number of credible threats to my safety, my family's safety, my staff's safety has risen dramatically. There's a lot of roots to that, but at the end of the day, that's a pretty high toll, and that's one set of reasons. Another thing that makes it easier for me to make this decision is that I feel like we've done an incredible amount of good work in seven and a half years. I'm really proud of the work that “Team City” has done, whether that's bus rapid transit or the incredible amount of housing that we've catalyzed through changes to our zoning and through our affordable housing fund. We've done some really good work on climate and particularly the intersection of affordability and climate that we don't maybe talk about as much as we should. But I think we have some great programs running that I'm really proud of. We've built a really strong team at the city. We have some incredible public servants. I feel like I'm ready for a different type of work. I'm ready for a different challenge where I'm not necessarily the face of all of it, where I can do good work for my community — whatever level of community that is — and not get personally attacked on a daily basis. Earlier this week, at the end of a 12-hour city council meeting, alders voted to fire Madison's independent monitor. That position was created by the council to be a watchdog on the police department during your [mayoral] tenure, along with the Police Civilian Oversight Board. That meeting was the longest and most contentious council meeting I've covered. You were the target of some of the comments. What do you make of the meeting and the council's decision? A little bit of a side note, but we actually looked it up today. The meeting on the [redevelopment of the] Edgewater Hotel under Mayor Dave Cieslewicz was actually longer. Not as controversial or loud, but longer, which I thought was very interesting. [The Oct. 20 meeting] was an incredibly tough meeting. From the very beginning, I think the question of police oversight in Madison has been complicated. [Our office was] actively working on what the best structure for police oversight would be when members of the city council, for whatever reason, decided they didn't want the mayor's office involved and they wanted to create a committee and do it themselves. They're the legislative branch of the city. They have every right to do that. I'm not complaining about that. But I do think that if there had been somebody from the executive branch involved in that conversation, we would have been able to point out some of the structural issues that we are now seeing play out. But the council made it very clear that was their thing. They wanted to do it. They didn't want the mayor's office involved, and we have stayed not involved. I think city staff have really struggled. [The independent police monitor office doesn’t report to the mayor] but HR has to help them, right? IT has to support them. There's been a lot of lack of clarity. I hope that going forward we can have a more collaborative process, not just with the executive branch, but with the community, and most importantly, with national experts, to make whatever changes are necessary to our ordinances and the system that the council set up, so that we can have more successful civilian oversight in the future because we've had different versions of unsuccessful. I don't want us to have just a third version of unsuccessful. Madison deserves this. We need it, but we need it to function. I think there's a lot of work to do. One more question on this, and then I want to talk more about you. So that council meeting, you could feel the heartbreak and the, I think, justified anger in the room… Absolutely, yeah. …over Corey Ruiz, who was killed three months ago today by Madison police. You have been frequently criticized for not visiting the Willy Street vigil and encampment which sprung up at the intersection where he was killed, before making the decision to clear it. Why did you stay away? I didn't want it to be about me, and I knew that if I went, it would be. I watched other politicians go down, and it was 100% about them. I don't think that's right. It was about Corey. It was about the community. It was about the grief and anger that people were feeling. I did not think that it would lead us anywhere positive for me to interrupt that. I think the feeling behind that is, and I think we saw it in the council chambers as well, is that people deeply want to feel like somebody cares about them, and that the physical presence somehow is a stand-in for “you care about me.” You can care about somebody and not be present physically. I think there are portions of our community that are in deep pain, and this is one of the things that I struggle with every day. I've been thinking about the role of city government in bringing a community together, to wrestle with hard issues in a way that recognizes everybody's humanity, since the pandemic. I don't have any answers. It's something that I struggle with regularly, and I look to other communities. What are other governments doing? What are non-governmental organizations doing? What I see is us drifting farther and farther apart from each other. Whether that's because of our media bubbles, or the time we spend on the screen, or the deep fear rooted out in the pandemic, or the impact of our federal government. I think there's a lot of things going on. Even here in Madison, we have forgotten how to productively talk to each other, and across differences, and I think that I just see that showing up again and again. Have you seen that nature of discourse change in the time that you've been mayor? Absolutely. At the council meeting, there were all sorts of insults and rumors thrown at you. I've never seen anything that bad, but yes. Even from the time I served on the city council, it has gotten exponentially worse, and it is not about a position on an issue. It is not about Democrat versus Republican or progressive versus conservative. Everybody is behaving poorly. I see roots in our current president, in his behavior and what he's normalized. I see roots in the pandemic. The pandemic made everybody afraid. People don't like to feel afraid, and many people transmuted that into anger. But also, we forgot how to be around other human beings during the pandemic. I really do blame social media for a lot of this, for misinformation and disinformation and the creation of a bubble via algorithm that makes you think that everybody agrees with you. That encourages tribalism. All of that is playing out in Madison. It doesn't follow national political divides but it's all happening here, too. Let's talk more about what comes next? You have six months left in your term. Are there final projects that you want to accomplish before leaving office? We have a whole spreadsheet [laughs]. There are things we're working on that I want to finish. There are things I want to move a step forward, even if we don't get to finish them. It spans the gamut from moving the Amtrak project another step forward, at least. I won't see that through, but would like to get everything set up for success. There's some administrative procedure memoranda that I think need to be updated. Geeky inside-government stuff that I think would make processes work better or make staff more efficient. We've still got a few things on housing that we want to try and move forward. Those geeky government things are a lot of being a mayor or a public official. You literally studied how to be a mayor while serving as managing director at the Mayor's Innovation Project. You also served as an alder before running for mayor. After spending nearly eight years in this position, how is the idea or perception of being mayor different from actually doing it? That's an excellent question. It is so different. I probably had the best preparation that you could have to be mayor, having studied city governments for over a decade and working directly with mayors, watching them work. I came into office, and I mean, I'm a policy wonk, right? So I was really excited about all this good policy stuff. I remember in literally my first week in office, I had two “ Aha! ” moments. When I was on the city council, I probably saw 30% of what goes on in city government, and there's this whole other 70% that I just had no idea about. Not that anybody's hiding anything, but just that if you're not doing it every day, you don't see everything that happens or all of this work that goes on every single day. The other realization I had was, oh, my job is not policy. My job is managing people and creating a budget, and that was a big wake-up call for me. I have gotten to do some policy. But mostly, I have gotten to do it by talking with experts on staff or outside experts in coming up with the idea, and staff are actually doing the policy writing. When I was at university, I got to do the policy research and writing. I do think that the primary job of a mayor in Madison — and I don't think the public sees this — is that you are the CEO of a 3,000-person corporation. It is your job to get the work done, take care of your employees, make sure they have the resources to do the work that they need to do for the community. Yes, you set the direction. You steer the ship. But your job is not kissing babies and cutting ribbons. Your job is managing people. The other huge piece is there is so much work that goes into the budget before it even hits the finance committee. There are big decisions to be made about what the city budget is going to look like every year. There's quite a wide field of people running for mayor. Probably more after this. It probably will get wider, yeah. Is there anyone you're supporting? No. I don't, at the moment, plan to endorse anyone. Certainly not right away. I do think it's a wide field. It may get wider. I think I'd want to let that settle out before I made any decision. What advice do you have for the next mayor? I am keeping a list. I do think the first and most obvious question, and this is really for the candidates, not for the next mayor, is: Are you sure you want to do this? It is a 24-hour job, and there are parts about it that are amazing, and very rewarding, and at least for me, very interesting. I've learned a tremendous amount. But it is a very hard job, and anybody who's running has to ask themselves, and maybe more importantly, their family, if they're up for it. For the next mayor, I think my advice would be very much along the lines of what we just talked about — your job, primarily, is to manage people, and to give them the resources they need to get the job done, so that's what you should be focused on. You should be focused on building a strong team, hiring good people if you have the opportunity to, and supporting them to do a good job. I mean, that's a very sort of internal aspect of it. There is obviously the external aspect of it. For that, setting a vision that’s realistic but aspirational and communicating that to the city, and working with partners to help bring people on board. One of the things that I've really enjoyed is discovering the other leaders in town that can be good partners. Whether that's the school superintendent or the head of the United Way, or the UW-Madison chancellor, or the president of Madison College. There’s a lot of folks, a lot of institutions in this town that work together, sometimes publicly, but often quietly behind the scenes, to make the community a better place. That is another aspect of the job that I think is really important: to have good relationships. It’s one of the things that I'm really proud of. I don't know if it's small or not, but former County Executive [Joe] Parisi and I broke the “curse of the fourth floor,” and actually created a relationship where the mayor and county exec not only talked to each other and met regularly, but actually worked together. And County Executive [Melissa] Agard and I have continued that. I really hope that the next person who sits in this office will keep that going, because the city and county are both better when we're working together. I obviously have a lot of advice. I don't know if the person who comes next will want to hear any of it, and I certainly will not force it on them. But I've always liked the supposed tradition of leaving a letter for whoever comes next, and I think I'll do that. I'll also be available. I'll tell you one thing I'm not going to do, though, apologies to Isthmus : I'm not going to write a blog. Fair enough. Where would you like to work next? Will you run for another elected office or take another public-facing role? I don't know. I don't have any firm plans. I don't think I will run for office anytime soon. I wouldn't rule it out for the rest of my life, but I don't have any plans to. That doesn't mean that I wouldn't be interested in serving in government in some role. I think that's certainly a possibility. I think academia is also a possibility, but I'm not ruling anything out. I am hopeful that I'll get to take a little break, and then, who knows? It's mid-April 2027, you wake up and don’t have to go to the City-County Building. What are you going to do? How are you going to spend that time? There is the super prosaic stuff, like I'm going to actually pull my weight around the house. I'm going to go through the stacks of boxes of stuff that [my partner] Amy would really like me to get rid of. I'm hoping to spend more time with my family and travel with them. I have four nephews and one niece, who I don't see enough of. My parents are aging. I don't see enough of them either. I would really like to spend more time traveling. I'm not going to have any trouble filling my days, but I'm also really excited about the possibility of using my brain in a different way. When I was at the Mayor's Innovation Project, I enjoyed researching and writing about policy. Even way back before that, I really enjoyed teaching. So yeah. I'm gonna try and find something that's at least as fun as being mayor.

title: City, state employees are proud of their work but face burnout, harassment - apg-wi.com
text: State and local government employees report high levels of job satisfaction across the country, but face significant rates of burnout and on-the-job harassment. That’s according to a new national survey of nearly 5,000 public servants across all 50 states released last week by The People Lab at Harvard University’s Kennedy School. Researchers say the survey, which includes respondents from hundreds of local governments, provides the nation’s most comprehensive analysis of workplace conditions in local governments. Most employees reported high levels of job satisfaction: 82% said they were at least somewhat satisfied with their job, while 60% said they were satisfied or very satisfied. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she is dropping reelection bid “That’s good news that people are still kind of proud to say they work for the government,” said Elizabeth Linos, faculty director of The People Lab. But 40% of employees also reported experiencing at least one symptom of burnout. And 27% said they intended to leave their jobs in the next 12 months. “You have such a big portion of your public sector workforce that are burnt out on any given day,” Linos said. “…And it’s not the pandemic and it’s not a particular crisis, so to me that says a lot about how much work we have to do to support our public servants.” State employees consistently reported less favorable workforce conditions than their city and county counterparts, with lower satisfaction, lower engagement and a substantially higher intent to leave. The study initially aimed to survey local government employees, so it includes results from only about 320 state employees, compared with more than 4,400 employees in city, county and other local governments. Linos said future analyses would include more state employees to better understand the distinctions between levels of government. She expects the research may mirror polling on public perception of government , which finds people report more faith in their local governments than the federal government. “You could imagine a world where being able to see the impact of your work more directly leads to more workplace satisfaction than if you have to kind of make the case for how your work has impact, if you work at higher levels of government,” she said. In the survey, 35% of employees reported experiencing harassment at work over the past year, defined as being bullied, threatened, attacked or harassed. That included 22% who reported harassment from internal sources such as coworkers or supervisors, while 17% reported harassment from external sources such as residents or the media. Those who reported harassment were far more likely to report emotional exhaustion at work and intentions to leave their jobs. Harassment levels were higher among local government employees and employees who identified as female, non-binary or other gender. Among those who shared their political party affiliation, Republican and Democratic public servants reported more favorable workforce conditions than independents across nearly every measure. Linos said the results should inform policymakers and government leaders alike. Every societal challenge — from transportation to climate change to housing — relies on a functioning public sector, she said. “The people of government, to me, are the central component of that capacity,” she said. “So if we don’t understand and appreciate the work that the people of government do, we’re not going to be able to solve the bigger public policy challenges that we’re trying to solve, and oftentimes that work is hidden from the public.”

text: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway will not seek re-election, she announced in a blog post Friday afternoon . “I am immensely proud of what I and my team have achieved over the past seven and a half years as we have worked to make Madison a better place and to prepare the path for future success,” she wrote. “My tenure has been marked by unprecedented challenges including COVID-19 and a state legislature intent on taking away our funding and powers. Despite the challenges, we achieved a great deal for those who choose to make Madison home.” Rhodes-Conway had announced in July that she would seek a third term. About a week later, Madison police shot and killed Corey Ruiz. Rhodes-Conway faced sharp criticism for her response. She declined to visit the site of the shooting, which became home to a memorial gathering that lasted 12 days, until City staff and police cleared it on the morning of August 4 at the mayor’s direction. More recently, she drew criticism for declining to provide condolences to Ruiz’s mother at a Common Council meeting where Elsa Ruiz testified against the termination of the interim independent police monitor. “During my remaining time in office, I hope that we can all take a hard look at our local political ecosystem,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Madison has long been home to impassioned and spirited debate. But it is not hyperbole to say local democracy is at risk, not just from MAGA and right-wing extremists in the federal and state governments, but from a toxic political culture that is transcending partisanship and ideology. “Harassment, threats, and lack of civility are driving people away from public service,” she added. Rhodes-Conway joined the Madison Common Council as an alder in 2007, succeeding Brian Benford when he decided not to run for re-election. She served two terms, stepping away in 2013. She defeated incumbent Mayor Paul Soglin in 2019, and won re-election over former deputy mayor and school board president Gloria Reyes in 2023. In June 2020, at the height of protests following the police murder of George Floyd, she recorded a video expressing sympathy for and gratitude for the police and posted it to a password-protected section of the City website. The video was leaked and posted to a pro-police Facebook group, and Rhodes-Conway apologized in a statement. Rhodes-Conway’s exit from the race still leaves a crowded field, including former Alders Benford and Sayed Abbas, One City Schools founder Kaleem Caire, former Dane County Board supervisor April Kigeya, former Golden Gloves boxer Marcus Robert Johnson, visual artist and activist Natalia Hacerola, Monkey Bar Gym founder Jonny Hinds, and Larry “Ace” Williams. The primary is set for February 16, and the two candidates with the most votes will face off in the general election on April 6. Rhodes-Conway said that Madison’s continued progress requires good government and serious engagement from our community. “We need leaders who are more interested in making the government function well than in performing for social media. We need leaders who want to continuously improve, but won’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good. We need leaders who are able to listen to and balance a wide range of voices. Above all, we need leaders who put the needs of Madison before their popularity or political futures,” she said. Madison365 is a news outlet covering communities of color in Wisconsin.

New national research found high levels of job satisfaction among public employees, but high levels of burnout and harassment at work. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) State and local government employees report high levels of job satisfaction across the country, but face significant rates of burnout and on-the-job harassment. That’s according to a new national survey of nearly 5,000 public servants across all 50 states released last week by The People Lab at Harvard University’s Kennedy School. Researchers say the survey, which includes respondents from hundreds of local governments, provides the nation’s most comprehensive analysis of workplace conditions in local governments. Most employees reported high levels of job satisfaction: 82% said they were at least somewhat satisfied with their job, while 60% said they were satisfied or very satisfied. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she is dropping reelection bid “That’s good news that people are still kind of proud to say they work for the government,” said Elizabeth Linos, faculty director of The People Lab. But 40% of employees also reported experiencing at least one symptom of burnout. And 27% said they intended to leave their jobs in the next 12 months. “You have such a big portion of your public sector workforce that are burnt out on any given day,” Linos said. “…And it’s not the pandemic and it’s not a particular crisis, so to me that says a lot about how much work we have to do to support our public servants.” State employees consistently reported less favorable workforce conditions than their city and county counterparts, with lower satisfaction, lower engagement and a substantially higher intent to leave. The study initially aimed to survey local government employees, so it includes results from only about 320 state employees, compared with more than 4,400 employees in city, county and other local governments. Linos said future analyses would include more state employees to better understand the distinctions between levels of government. She expects the research may mirror polling on public perception of government , which finds people report more faith in their local governments than the federal government. “You could imagine a world where being able to see the impact of your work more directly leads to more workplace satisfaction than if you have to kind of make the case for how your work has impact, if you work at higher levels of government,” she said. In the survey, 35% of employees reported experiencing harassment at work over the past year, defined as being bullied, threatened, attacked or harassed. That included 22% who reported harassment from internal sources such as coworkers or supervisors, while 17% reported harassment from external sources such as residents or the media. Harassment levels were higher among local government employees and employees who identified as female, non-binary or other gender. title: A sad day in Madison - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: Chali Pittman Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would run for a third term about a week before the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. I wasn’t too surprised that Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway decided not to run for re-election after all. But I was shocked and saddened by her reason. The mayor announced her bid for a third term in July, but her heart didn’t seem to be in it. She never filed the official declaration of candidacy and she didn’t do what serious candidates do: work the phones to raise money. So, I thought she might not run because her early announcement did not scare off contenders. There are several of them. But the reason she gave for retiring had nothing to do with that. She revealed that she, her family and her staff have been on the receiving end of personal harassment and even what are apparently credible death threats. She wasn’t specific about where those are coming from, but we know that her home was strewn with yard signs and pamphlets following the police shooting of Corey Ruiz on Willy Street in late July, about a week after she announced her reelection bid. And we also know that the council meeting which resulted in the firing of interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass was among the most uncivil and raw in recent memory. Rhodes-Conway announced her decision to pull the plug on her campaign less than two days after that meeting. The mayor correctly pointed out a number of significant accomplishments during her two terms. These include bus rapid transit, a new men’s homeless shelter, new teams of mental health professionals to respond to some calls that might otherwise go to police, and progress on green energy. My own view is that her greatest accomplishment was an aggressive pro-development agenda that has resulted in some 20,000 new housing units in the city since she took office. And, in fact, that has been another source of controversy for the mayor, though I’m not aware that it has resulted in the kind of harassment she called out in her statement. For decades we’ve talked in general terms about the need for “infill” housing. Virtually all of us agree that it is better to grow up than out into some of the richest farmland in the world. But when infill actually happens a lot of neighbors want to clarify their support for it: the building they support was supposed to take place in someone else’s backyard. Rhodes-Conway took the heat and stayed the course. In fact, BRT and its related zoning overlays are designed to create even more density in the future. She has put the city on the right track for our future, but she was paying the short-term political price for it. Like all mayors, Rhodes-Conway learned that you get it from both sides. In the case of the Ruiz shooting, police reform activists blamed her for not coming down on their side while residents and businesses in the Willy Street neighborhood said she waited too long to move on the protest encampment at the site of the incident. In the case of the police monitor she had a management mess on her hands that she had little direct control over thanks to the odd way in which the ordinance was constructed. Unlike every other city manager she had virtually no control over this position. So, much of what she has experienced is par for the course. But in my eight years on the job, from 2003 to 2011, I had all of one death threat. The police made contact with the guy and concluded he wasn’t credible and that was the end of it. Sure, I had my share of angry people, I took my share of vitriol and the personal attack from time to time, but I never once felt physically unsafe. Nobody ever harassed my family or my staff or protested at my house. What brought Rhodes-Conway to this decision is only a reflection of what’s happened to our politics in the last decade and a half. We can blame much of this on Donald Trump and how he has crushed every standard of human decency imaginable. But we can’t forget that over 70 million of our fellow Americans voted for him. Three times. And all the while knowing the kind of man he is. What really concerns me is that, beyond the MAGA hard core, there are so many of us who see who this man is and do not find his character (or lack of it) disqualifying. I don’t blame the mayor for deciding it’s time to find another way to make a contribution. The message she has sent us on her way out is something we need to take to heart. We may not have a big MAGA problem in Madison, but we’ve got our own forms of rampant hostility. We can’t go on like this. Dave Cieslewicz is a Madison- and Upper Peninsula-based writer who served as mayor of Madison from 2003 to 2011. You can read more of his work at Yellow Stripes & Dead Armadillos .

By Dustin Robertson , Raveena John , October 28, 2026 With midterm elections next week, we’re looking back at successful Complete Streets ballot measures in recent years. These wins show that safer, more accessible streets are a winning issue across the country and offer lessons for candidates and advocates on how to build a successful campaign. Learn more about our Complete Streets work here. With elections happening across the country next week, we thought it would be a good time to let everyone know that Complete Streets can be a political winner. Political topics and election issues shift over time, but we have seen time and time again that Complete Streets (or its components) can be very successful in local elections. You don’t have to take our word for it, though. Here are four recent wins by Complete Streets candidates and Complete Streets ballot measures. From these successes, readers should feel inspired to think about how they might be applied in their own communities. First elected in 2019, Mayor Rhodes-Conway ran for reelection in 2023 on a campaign that highlighted the transformation of the city’s transit networks under her leadership, including safe and accessible streets , bus rapid transit, and electric buses . “ was politically risky,” Rhodes-Conway said in a local news source . “I staked a lot on it. Like I told voters in the last election, I make decisions based on good public policy — not what’s politically expedient.” According to our recent research, Madison is one of the safest cities in the country for pedestrians . Rhodes-Conway was reelected with 55.2 percent of the vote. Lesson for candidates: Take risks, let results speak for themselves, and celebrate them. Transformative changes are daunting, but stand by strong policy choices so constituents can experience the positive results. Lesson for advocates: It’s easy to point out what a political leader is doing wrong, but if they do something you like, celebrate it and encourage them to do more! In 2024, Nashville passed a transportation referendum that created $3.1 billion in dedicated funding for transit service, sidewalk projects, street improvements, signal upgrades, and other improvements. With 66 percent of the vote, the strong support for this initiative was a significant reversal from a previously attempted transportation referendum, “Let’s Move Nashville,” which lost by 64 percent in 2018. This piece from Transportation for America shows the key factors that made Choose How You Move successful, including strong leadership from the mayor and a broad coalition of supportive organizations and community groups. Choose How You Move includes investments in 39 miles of Complete Streets projects, with a focus on the streets most in need of safety improvements. Lesson for candidates: Think broad and build strong coalitions. One of the reasons the 2018 referendum failed was that there was not enough public engagement, including with Nashville’s Black faith community. It’s important to think of all the stakeholders who could benefit from Complete Streets initiatives, and engage them early and often. Lesson for advocates: Previous setbacks should not inhibit your efforts. Nashville showed that within just a few years, voters’ minds can change. Learn from previous efforts and keep building! Four years after she was first elected District 8 County Commissioner in 2020, Myers ran for reelection on a platform based on her support for Complete Streets. Building on her work co-writing the Athens Complete Streets Ordinance, supporting a residential traffic management program, and advocating for Vision Zero funding, among other actions, her reelection platform included “Walkability! Bike lanes! Better buses! Safer streets!” She won reelection with 72.5 percent of the vote. Lesson for candidates: Build on your success–Complete Streets can help champions win elections and get reelected. Lesson for advocates: Support candidates who champion and deliver on Complete Streets. The energy, enthusiasm, and exclamation points in Commissioner Myers’ campaign show how popular these issues likely are within the community. Thanks to strong advocacy by Denver Streets Partnership , the people of Denver said “yes” in 2022 to building a safe and complete sidewalk network. Passing with 56 percent of the vote, Citizen-Initiated Ordinance 307 moved the responsibility and cost of building and maintaining sidewalks from property owners to the city. It also sped up the timeline for sidewalk expansion and ongoing maintenance through a dedicated annual property fee. But this victory did not happen easily or overnight: Denver Streets Partnership worked for years to improve the city’s sidewalks. After incremental gains from earlier efforts , the organization decided to take the issue directly to voters. They collected 20,000 signatures to get Denver Deserves Sidewalks on the ballot and gathered endorsements from a wide variety of organizations and groups. Now, the city is developing its first Sidewalk Implementation Plan , a roadmap to carrying out these popular, much-needed improvements. Lesson for candidates: Complete Streets can win elections, even if it will cost voters money. By presenting the numerous benefits of a truly complete and connected sidewalk network, Denver Deserves Sidewalks supporters were able to convince voters to support the ordinance. Lesson for advocates: Persistence pays off. Denver Deserves Sidewalks was the result of years of advocacy and work by Denver Streets Partnership and other Complete Streets champions. Changing minds of both voters and decisionmakers can take time, but consistent efforts make Complete Streets victories possible. Across the country, there’s broad consensus and support for Complete Streets because of their role in creating safe, healthy, and prosperous communities. They have proven to be an election winner in red states, blue states, and coast to coast. It’s true that a few vocal opponents (e.g., NIMBYs) can disrupt important projects, but the beauty of democracy is that everyone has a voice, and safer, more walkable communities are something that most people agree on. title: What’s on the Madison ballot for midterm elections? - The Daily Cardinal
text: Election Day for midterm races across the nation is Nov. 3. Here’s what you will see when casting your ballot in Madison, Wisconsin.  Governor’s race The Democratic candidate Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and the Republican candidate U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany face off after Gov. Tony Evers left the seat open following his two terms.  The two candidates are paired on the same ticket with the nominees for lieutenant governor. Crowley runs on the ticket with current Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski, and Tiffany runs with Lancaster Mayor David Varnam. Attorney General Incumbent Democrat Josh Kaul faces a challenge from Republican Fond du Lac District Attorney Eric Toney. This is a rematch from 2022 when Kaul defeated Toney by just over one point for the seat that heads the Department of Justice.  Secretary of State Three candidates are vying for the open seat as Godlewski runs for lieutenant governor. Democrat Milwaukee Alder JoCasta Zamarripa , real estate investor Republican Jay Schroeder and former Racine Alder Peter Karas of the Green Party face off for the seat holding the state records and seal.  Treasurer Incumbent Republican John S. Leiber faces a challenge from Democrat Marathon County Supervisor Yee Leng Xiong. Wisconsin hasn’t reelected a state treasurer in over 20 years, and this seat signs checks and manages the state's trust fund. 2nd Congressional District Incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan is uncontested in his race for the U.S. House of Representatives. Pocan has held the seat since 2013. 76th Assembly District Voters on Madison’s east side will see this race on their ballot. Madison Alder Democrat Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford and Republican Nina Chat face off for the seat left open by Rep. Francesca Hong who ran and lost to Crowley in the Democratic primary for governor.  77th Assembly District Voters on Madison’s west side will see this race on their ballot. Incumbent Democrat state Rep. Renuka Mayadev faces a challenge from Republican Jane McCormick , a real estate broker. See which Assembly district you live in here . Dane County Sheriff Incumbent Democrat Kalvin D. Barrett is uncontested in this race.  Dane County Clerk Of Circuit Court Incumbent Democrat Jeff Okazaki is uncontested in this race. Constitutional amendments Three constitutional amendments appear on the ballot, all which are written and proposed by Republican lawmakers.  The first aims to end the governor’s partial veto powers. It states “Partial veto. Shall section 10 (1) (c) of article V of the constitution be amended to prohibit the governor, in exercising his or her partial veto authority, from creating or increasing or authorizing the creation or increase of any tax or fee?”  The second aims to allow people to gather in places of worship during declared emergencies. It states “Freedom to gather in places of worship during an emergency. Shall section 18 of article I of the constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency?" The third aims to prohibit governmental discrimination race, sex, ethnicity or national origin, like affirmative action. It states "Governmental entity discrimination prohibited. Shall section 27 of article I of the constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration?" Early voting on campus is held at the School of Nursing, School of Human Ecology and Union South from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. and at Memorial Union from 11:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. until Oct. 30. Day-of polling places and more voting information can be found here . Election Day is set for Nov. 3. Audrey Lopez-Stane is the state news editor for The Daily Cardinal. She has written in-depth on free speech on campus, agriculture and elections including the Wisconsin Supreme Court race and 2026 midterm elections. Audrey previously interned at WisPolitics and now works for Wisconsin Watch. Follow her on X @ALopezStane .

title: Madison Finances Hold Steady Post-Referendum, Enable New Investments - wnanews.com
text: Weekly Fiscal Facts are provided to Wisconsin NewsMedia Association members by the  Wisconsin Policy Forum , the state’s leading resource for nonpartisan state and local government research and civic education. The Wisconsin Policy Forum logo can be downloaded here . Two years after Madison voters approved a $22 million property tax increase for the city in a referendum, the city’s finances, services, and infrastructure remain in a relatively strong position. According to the Wisconsin Policy Forum’s annual brief on the city of Madison’s next proposed budget, it would limit the property tax levy increase to roughly the recent rate of inflation while protecting the transit system and bolstering services in some areas. The city benefits from rates of new construction that generally outpace the state average, low unemployment rates in Dane County, and a relatively strong economy. For a Midwest city in 2026, Madison remains in an enviable position. This enables Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway to make new investments in her 2027 budget proposal, which will be taken up by the Madison Common Council in coming weeks. It provides raises for city employees and fully funds a new ambulance company and new library on the city’s northeast side. With the help of a $350,000 grant from the Madison Community Foundation, the budget would implement body cameras for most Madison police officers. And city reserves would remain well above target levels, providing ample fiscal cushion. At the same time, the city’s budget shows some signs of pressure. Relatively rapid growth in spending and tight limits on local revenues like the property tax are likely to open up gaps in future budgets, and a relatively fast-growing population means city staff and resources are being spread more thinly. The city also covered Madison Metro Transit’s operating shortfall in this budget with federal money that in part could otherwise be used for capital needs such as bus purchases. Under the mayor’s proposal, general and library fund spending would total $477.5 million in 2027, a 5.5% increase over the prior year. While not the largest recent increase for Madison, it would be more than last year’s budget and outpace the rate of inflation. Top areas of spending growth are for additional debt payments, as well as for the fire and police departments, primarily to give cost of living pay increases. The city property tax levy on December tax bills would grow to $337.9 million, an increase of $11.2 million, or 3.4%. That would be more than the prior year’s increase but still roughly the rate of inflation. Madison transit revenues still have yet to recover from the effects of the pandemic, making transit a key area to watch in this budget. The 12-month period from September 2025 to August 2026 marked the first post-pandemic year in which monthly average ridership topped 1 million riders, nearing the pre-COVID monthly average. However, revenue growth lags the growth in ridership and has not increased as much as expected. Revenue from sources including fares in 2027 is projected to remain 16.2% below 2019, before adjusting for inflation. To respond to the agency’s lingering funding challenges, the mayor’s 2027 budget includes a proposed $25.5 million transfer from the city’s general fund. Looking ahead, with the city’s East-West Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) line up and running, attention has now shifted to the proposed North-South line, currently in the final design phase. Yet this buildout comes with significant questions about the sustainability of Metro Transit funding. The budget also would maintain city reserves at very robust levels. However, the city’s long-term plan calls for them to be drawn down significantly – a move that could work for a few years, but could not be sustained indefinitely without major tradeoffs.
